q: Calculate the percentage of the oxygen carried that is unloaded at rest and when running.
Calculate the volume of oxygen delivered to the muscle each minute when running.
Unloaded per dm³ = 0.72 × 200 = 144 cm³. × 12 dm³ min⁻¹ = about 1730 cm³ min⁻¹.
At rest the muscle receives 44 cm³ of oxygen per minute. Calculate how many times more it receives when running.
1730 / 44 = about 39 times.
Using the shape of the dissociation curve, explain why a fall in muscle pO₂ from 3.5 to 2.0 kPa releases so much oxygen.
This is the steep part of the S-shaped curve: a small fall in pO₂ causes a large fall in saturation, because of cooperative binding (each O₂ released makes the next one easier to release).
Suggest two other changes in a running muscle that increase oxygen unloading.
Any two: more CO₂ and lower pH (Bohr shift); higher temperature; more lactate.

20.t: Working with data: CO₂ and saturation
q: Read the saturation at 4 kPa from each curve and calculate the difference.
Normal 72%, high CO₂ 52%: a difference of 20 percentage points.
Describe the effect of high pCO₂ on the curve.
The curve shifts to the right: lower saturation at each pO₂, except near 12 kPa where both are almost full.
Explain how CO₂ causes this shift.

CO₂ reacts with water (carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which releases H⁺. H⁺ binds to haemoglobin and changes its shape, lowering its affinity for oxygen; some CO₂ also binds haemoglobin directly.
Explain why the shift hardly affects oxygen loading in the lungs.
Lung pO₂ is about 12 kPa, the flat part of both curves, where saturation is 97–98% either way.
Suggest why the shift is an advantage during exercise.
Muscles respiring fastest make the most CO₂, so haemoglobin unloads most oxygen exactly where it is needed.
